extracted.intended_audience: poets, satirists, and students of poetic craft (readers of classical satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive observations and examples from Horace about composing, performing, and ethically framing satirical verse — covering style, revision, audience, and moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: License of satiric poets to brand vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient comic poets (Eupolis, Cratinus, Aristophanes) and Lucilius 'branded' rascals, thieves, adulterers, etc., with great freedom; satiric poets traditionally expose and name vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire historically has a broad license to denounce public vice and infamous behavior. Example: Horace endorses the comic practice of freely branding wrongdoers. Anti-pattern: treating satire as merely polite or timid criticism that avoids naming corrupt or vicious behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: True-poet requirement: genius and greatness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not call every versifier a poet: 'To him who has genius, who has a soul of a diviner cast, and a greatness of expression, give the honor of this appellation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for being a 'poet' is animated spirit and elevated expressive power, not mere technical versification. If the work lacks a lofty spirit and force it risks being mere prose in meter. Use this to judge whether a work attains poetic stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic force over mere versification (distinct from prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a verse, when taken to pieces or its word-order changed, becomes indistinguishable from prose, 'you will not discern the limbs of a poet' — true poetry must have an internal force that resists such disassembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem's diction, rhythm, and rhetorical energy create effects that transcend simple metrical arrangement. Example: Horace contrasts transposed, limp lines with Ennius's lines that retain poetic force. Anti-pattern: technically correct meter with no animating energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligent composition and revision; avoid verbosity and slovenliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucilius is criticized for being 'verbose, and too lazy to endure the fatigue of writing — of writing accurately' (dictating many verses quickly). Horace praises modest, meek disposition that speaks seldom and briefly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality requires careful drafting and revision; rapid, undisciplined production that sacrifices accuracy is a fault. Scoring note: reward careful editing, concise expression, and evidence of revision; penalize sloppy, over-long, or unpolished output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should avoid malice and personal revenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace denies being 'a common accuser' and rejects 'black malignity' — satire must not be mere personal spite or vindictive libel against acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the moral stance of the satire: is it attacking systemic or public vices for corrective ends, or settling private scores? Examples/anti-patterns: justified public censure vs. malicious gossip that uses satire to harm friends or acquaintances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical boundary: do not expose private secrets gratuitously
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace argues against publicizing private faults ('he who cannot keep secrets... is a dangerous man') and disavows turning the private reputations of intimates into public sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or producing satire, respect confidentiality and avoid gratuitous exposure of private matters. Preference given to satire that targets public behaviors and character types rather than intimate confidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic/moral purpose: use examples of others' disgrace to deter vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace describes how his father trained him by 'noting each particular vice I might avoid it by the example [of others]' — satire can serve to preserve traditional morality and deter destructive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether satirical elements are directed toward instructing or warning readers (didactic aim) rather than merely mocking. Effective satire often uses character exempla to teach or reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of recitation and audience-awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace criticizes indiscriminate reciters who 'recite their writings in the middle of the forum; and who [do it] while bathing' and notes that performance context (place/time) affects reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate suitability of delivery: timing, venue, and audience expectations matter. Anti-pattern: public performance at unseasonable times/places that suggests lack of tact or self-awareness; positive pattern: choosing contexts that respect audience and enhance effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone moderation and seeking indulgence for boldness
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace asks readers to 'favor me by your indulgence' if he speaks 'too freely' or 'too ludicrously'; a satirist may push boundaries but should temper tone and request forgiveness when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the writer balances bold critique with gracious tone or preemptive humility. A measured solicitation of reader indulgence can mitigate perceptions of cruelty; untempered audacity without craft may offend without instructing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity: do not value volume in place of merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace remarks of Lucilius's prodigious output ('two hundred verses in an hour') and says 'with regard to the quantity [of his works], I make no account of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poets, prioritize depth, craft, and effect rather than prolific but careless production. Reward concentrated, well-crafted pieces over bulk output produced with negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/factual warrant for accusations in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace challenges the idea that he maliciously invents calumny and insists accusations should be grounded: 'Is any one then your voucher, with whom I have lived?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether satirical claims rest on credible observation or are mere invention. Satire with grounded examples carries moral weight; pure invention for shock value risks unjust harm and weakens persuasive force.
